candidate.answerReason: Because \(n-(q+r)=99q\) is divisible by 11, the desired numbers are exactly the five-digit multiples of 11. Their multipliers run from 910 through 9090, giving 8181 numbers.

methods.label: Method 1: Count five-digit multiples
methods.explanation:
The quotient-remainder relation is
\[
n=100q+r,
\qquad 100\le q\le999,
\qquad 0\le r\le99.
\]
To connect the condition on \(q+r\) directly to \(n\), subtract:
\[
n-(q+r)=99q=11(9q).
\]
Their difference is a multiple of \(11\), so \(q+r\) is divisible by \(11\) if and only if \(n\) is divisible by \(11\).

The smallest five-digit multiple is \(10010=11\cdot910\), since \(11\cdot909=9999\). The largest is \(99990=11\cdot9090\), since \(11\cdot9091=100001\). Thus every qualifying number has the form \(11k\) for exactly one integer \(k\) from \(910\) through \(9090\). Every such multiplier gives a qualifying number, and different multipliers give different numbers. The count is therefore
\[
9090-910+1=\boxed{8181}.
\]
The answer is choice B.
methods.levelReason: An exact divisibility identity and inclusive counting of integer multipliers suffice; formal congruence notation is unnecessary.

methods.label: Method 2: Count remainders in blocks
methods.explanation:
Each five-digit number corresponds uniquely to a pair of integers
\[
100\le q\le999,
\qquad 0\le r\le99,
\]
through \(n=100q+r\). Conversely, every pair in these ranges gives a five-digit number. We can therefore count qualifying pairs without omission or repetition.

Fix any of the \(900\) possible quotients \(q\). Split the remainders from \(0\) through \(98\) into nine blocks:
\[
0\text{ through }10,\quad
11\text{ through }21,\quad\ldots,\quad
88\text{ through }98.
\]
Within each block, the values of \(q+r\) are \(11\) consecutive integers, so exactly one is divisible by \(11\). Thus these blocks give exactly nine successful remainders for every quotient, accounting for \(900\cdot9\) numbers.

The only remaining remainder is \(r=99\). Since \(99\) is divisible by \(11\), it works exactly when \(q\) is divisible by \(11\). Such quotients are \(11k\) with \(10\le k\le90\), giving \(90-10+1=81\) extra numbers. These have remainder \(99\), so none was counted in the earlier blocks. The total is
\[
900\cdot9+81=\boxed{8181},
\]
choice B.
